top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: Given clinical and methodological heterogeneity across designs, settings, and outcomes, we conducted a narrative synthesis. Where available, we report effect measures with 95% CIs and p-values. We did not perform formal small-study or publication-bias tests because no meta-analysis was undertaken; instead, we qualitatively appraised potential reporting/publication biases and reflected these concerns within GRADE. Results from secondary research (systematic reviews) were used for context only and were not recombined with primary studies to avoid double counting.

top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: Evidence suggests DA reduces GP workload and resource use (medications, imaging) while showing clinical outcomes similar to GP-referred pathways and no consistent signal of increased harms. Economic analyses from observational studies indicated neutral to moderate cost savings, though reliance on non-randomised data limits certainty.

top_evidence.section: Methods > Study Design And Reporting Framework
top_evidence.text: This systematic review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 [24]. In accordance with PRISMA, we prepared outcome-specific Summary of Findings tables (SoF) that collate study-level results per outcome and are provided as Additional Tables S1-S7. The protocol was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; ID 897ub; 15 August 2024, available at h t t p s : / / o s f . i o/ 8 9 7 u b / ) [25]. The completed PRISMA 2020 checklist is available in Additional file 1.

top_evidence.text: Observational NOS scores ranged 4-6/9 (low-moderate) [32-35, 39, 42, 44, 46, 47]. RCTs were generally of moderate methodological quality but had small sample sizes and few participating sites, with limited allocation concealment [36, 38, 40, 41, 48]. The distribution of methodological quality levels by appraisal tool (ROB 2.0, NOS) is displayed in Fig. 3.

top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: Data were extracted using a standardised form adapted from the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (version 6.3) [27], with pre-specified units/ scales (e.g., VAS 0-10 or 0-100, ODI 0-100, MSK-HQ 0-56, EQ-5D index) recorded as reported. Extracted items included authors, year, country, design, sample, intervention/comparator, outcomes, measurement tools, sources of funding, declared conflicts of interest, and key quantitative results. Participants were counted once per unique study or cohort to avoid double counting when the same cohort was reported across linked publications (e.g., primary study and linked economic evaluation) or contributed data to multiple outcomes. For transparency, all study-level quantitative results used to populate the SoF are reproduced verbatim in Additional Tables S1-S7, with units and time windows preserved. Two reviewers (MaF and EB) independently extracted data and reconciled discrepancies by consensus.

top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: Strengths include PRISMA-guided methods, multi-database search with prospective update to November 2025, double independent screening/appraisal, and use of validated tools (ROB 2.0, NOS, & GRADE). The breadth of health system contexts and organisational models covered also strengthens the external validity of the findings, particularly for health services research and policy-oriented interpretation. Limitations include heterogeneity of DA/FCP/triage models and outcomes, predominance of observational designs, small RCT samples, and short follow-up, which prevented a robust meta-analysis; potential publication/reporting biases are considered within the GRADE judgements. Fig. 4 GRADE certainty by study design Type of study Priorities include pragmatic RCTs and prospective cohorts in regulated systems, with adequate samples, long-term outcomes, and full economic evaluations [36, 37, 40, 41]; and studies on GP satisfaction, collaboration, and patient acceptability [15, 16]. Future research should also adopt mixed-methods designs to better capture contextual factors influencing implementation, including organisational readiness and interprofessional dynamics. Such approaches are essential to inform policy decisions in systems where DA is introduced incrementally rather than through wholesale reform.

top_evidence.text: Outcome-level certainty was graded with Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE): risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, publication bias, indirectness [30]; Given the narrative synthesis without pooled estimates and the heterogeneity of outcomes precluding outcome-level aggregation, GRADE judgements were applied at the study level as inputs to the overall synthesis, consistent with guidance for reviews without meta-analysis. Economic evaluations published separately inherited the parent RCT's certainty rating. Dual independent grading (MaF and EB) with consensus.
